catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-1-q1.explanation: A - representsVerb ‘equals’ would need a ‘to’ preposition following it to fit. Other verbs do not fit here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-1-q2.explanation: D - switchingThe meaning of the gerund here is ‘moving or changing to’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-1-q3.explanation: D - consumptionThe meaning of the phrase is that the usage of ink will be reduced. ‘Consumption’ is a more formal word for ‘usage’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-1-q4.explanation: B - basisA synonymous phrase would be ‘working on that principle or starting point’. The idea is to apply same concept of using a different typeface at a larger scale, not just in one school.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-1-q5.explanation: C - interestinglyIt is interesting that the question had been brought up before but nothing was done.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-1-q6.explanation: A - issueAn issue here is used in the meaning of ‘unresolved matter or problem’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-1-q8.explanation: B - retainedA rather difficult choice; to retain means ‘to hold intact, to secure, to keep’

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-2-q9.explanation: whyThe author is clearly puzzled by the situation he finds himself in or doubts his motives of doing that.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-2-q10.explanation: but/except/besidesA paddle is the only thing the author has in his hands.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-2-q11.explanation: likeA comparison between two activities is made: paddle-boarding and canoeing.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-2-q12.explanation: doesTeacher’s reassurance has no effect on the narrator. It does nothing to him.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-2-q13.explanation: myNo article is needed here as ‘balance’ is an abstract noun

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-2-q14.explanation: on‘On the move’ means ‘in a state of moving, in motion’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-2-q15.explanation: despiteA negative preposition is needed to show contrast between the author’s action and its result

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-2-q16.explanation: otherwiseNot rowing on both sides results in going in circles.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-3-q17.explanation: enduranceEndurance is one’s ability to withstand (stand up against, to resist) difficulties.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-3-q18.explanation: doubtless/undoubtedlyContext suggest a negative form, which can be achieved by either a prefix or a suffix.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-3-q19.explanation: tolerantThe sentence that follows the gap helps us understand that the adjective required is a positive one: ‘We accept without question…’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-3-q21.explanation: usefulnessNot to be confused with ‘usage’, which is the way we use something; usefulness is how handy (useful) something is.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-3-q22.explanation: accessibleMake sure to use the right suffix -ible, not -able.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-3-q23.explanation: anxietiesAn anxiety is a state of nervousness and uneasiness, usually about something that is going to happen soon.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-3-q24.explanation: hopefullyThe author shows desire for maths to become more popular among people.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-4-q25.explanation: ‘leave out’ needs to be rephrased using the key word any. The correct transformation is ‘not to include any of’, where ‘include’ acts as a direct synonym of ‘leave out’ in a negative structure. The use of ‘any’ requires the construction ‘any of’ before a plural noun.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-4-q26.explanation: We are reporting an apology statement here. We move away from the gerund structuer ‘being unable’ a finite clause with a modal verb, while preserving the meaning and maintaining a formal register.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-4-q27.explanation: Used idiomatically, ‘lose sight of’ here means that the person has completely forgotten about something.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-4-q28.explanation: We use a so called ‘concessive clause’ here. This structure is used to emphasise that the degree of effort does not affect the outcome. The answer ‘and it does not matter how hard’ is grammatically fine, but it exceeds the six word limit we have in CAE Use of English Part 4.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-4-q29.answer: comes across to his boss as
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-4-q29.explanation: The phrasal verb ‘come across as’ is used to describe how a person appears to others.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-4-q30.answer: made no reference to; didn’t/did not make reference to
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-4-q30.explanation: One of the things we do is a verb-to-noun transformation. ‘To make a reference to’ is a common collocation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-5-q31.explanation: CThe answer can be found in the middle of Paragraph One: ‘In it she sounds suspiciously like a copywriter from her father’s media team.’. This suggests that the executive’s daughter has nothing to do with, but instead at attempt to make the change more ‘human’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-5-q32.explanation: C‘To set aside’ means to disregard or ignore; not to consider something

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-5-q33.explanation: DIn Paragraph Two a comparison between two companies is made to show how different they are and to hint at the possibility of a particular approach working for a smaller company is likely to fail if applied to a bigger one.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-5-q34.explanation: BAnswer A is mentioned, but only as a supporting point to the main argument. Answers C and D are not mentioned. From second sentence onwards, the author brings up a number of points that show how many factors are to be considered when taking a leave, and how they add up to make going on leave nearly impossible.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-5-q35.explanation: BFirst three sentences of Paragraph Four illustrate a number of situations when office workers can affect each other’s performance, choice and behaviour. Answer C is mentioned but in a different form and as a minor form to support the main argument. Answers A and D are not mentioned.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-5-q36.explanation: CThe key notion of the paragraph is in the second half, starting with the sentence ‘However, a potentially problematic corollary…’. The author then shows how the conventional application of work and rest policy proves to be more effective and how important periods of leisure are for the employees’ well-being. Other answers can be connected with the minor details in the first part of the paragraph, the purpose of which is to introduce the main argument in the second part.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-6-q37.explanation: DIn both paragraphs its respective authors mention Fernyhough combining scientific findings with his own experience in the matter. Paragraph B: ‘Fernyhough sees the emerging science of memory through the lens of his own recollections’; Paragraph D: ‘He mixes the latest findings in neuroscience with in-depth case histories. Nor is Fernyhough uncomfortable using personal testimony to put warm flesh on hard science: sizeable sections of the book are taken up with him exploring his own past.’

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-6-q38.explanation: DAll other reviewers are fond of the writer’s style. However, Reviewer D holds an opposite view. Second half of the paragraph: ‘This weariness is reflected in his writing style.’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-6-q39.explanation: ALast paragraph of Reviewer C text has a positive opinion of the author’s ability to mix literature and science. Reviewer A concurs in the second half of their text: ‘… sophisticated and engaging blend of findings from science, ideas from literature’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-6-q40.explanation: CReviewer D doesn’t feel that the author’s narration of personal experience benefits the book: ‘… sizeable sections of the book are taken up with him exploring his own past. These do not add greatly to the book…’. Reviewer C holds the same opinion: ‘… these autobiographical passages are the least successful of Pieces of Light…’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-7-q41.explanation: C‘These endeavors’ refers to the plans to renovate the dinosaur hall. The rest of the paragraph continues the subject started in the previous sentence – the planned restoration of that particular museum area.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-7-q42.explanation: GIs it easier to pick the right paragraph if we look at the next one after the gap. Paragraph G talks about multiple Allosaurus in different museum, then the following paragraph points out how Smithsonian’s Allosaurus is a special one.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-7-q43.explanation: DThe preceding paragraph mentions plans to disassemble the skeleton, then Paragraph D brings up the point of making the skeleton smaller and gives detailed explanation why and how they plan to achieve that.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-7-q44.explanation: F‘Mistake’ is the keyword here. The mistake that is mentioned in Paragraph F is the length of the dinosaur’s tail, which consist of too many bone segments. Same sentence continues with idea of finding out the dinosaur’s age, which is then continued in the paragraph that follows.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-7-q45.explanation: AAnother keyword in the gapped paragraph is ‘injury’. Then the paragraph below the topic of damages is expanded upon: ‘ … an apparent blow to the Allosaurus’s left side. ‘The shoulder blade looks like it has healed improperly,’ he explains.’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-7-q46.explanation: EThe word ‘suspicion’ in the last paragraph helps us to pick Paragraph E which focuses on a confusion between two species.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q47.explanation: CIn the second sentence a comparison between books and movies is made, with the former giving a certain degree of control of how we see things presented to us.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q48.explanation: BGiving examples of Tolstoy, Proust and Hardy, the author admits to having incomplete knowledge of the matter.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q49.explanation: DMiddle of the paragraph quotes a well-known writer, who warns people against not reading as it leads to poor imagination and narrower outlook on life.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q50.explanation: CThe author uses the word ‘assessors’, or those who evaluate the quality of (in this case) works of literature. Their perception of quality changes with the time period they come from.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q51.explanation: AThe word ‘escapism’ is used to justify picking a generic novel over an acclaimed masterpiece at the beginning of this paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q52.explanation: BSecond half of Paragraph B goes: ‘A work of fiction can always be fine-tuned …’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q53.explanation: DFirst two sentences of Paragraph D claim there is nothing bad about preferring a certain genre or author at any given period of a person’s life.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q54.explanation: BSecond sentence dismisses the notion of you having to put yourself under pressure to finish ‘a classic’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q55.explanation: CThe author of this paragraph shares Albert Camus’ opinion on why literature and reading are so appealing.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test16-part-8-q56.explanation: BLast sentence of the paragraph claims ‘trashy romances’ to be of less value than one work of classics, defending their opinion by ‘I’m going to go ahead and say it’s so anyway’.
